item.source_title: Al Ries and Laura Ries, The 22 Immutable Laws of Branding (HarperBusiness, 2002 combined edition)
item.source_locator: printed pp. 31-33 (Ch. 6, the Datastream case and 'never forget leadership')
item.question: A company leads a market that is currently tiny and its board wants to drop leadership messaging and sell the benefits of the category instead. Apply the authors' position, including what they say about the sophisticated customers such a strategy will lose.
item.answer: They would keep the leadership claim and reject the board's reasoning, which they state and dismiss in the chapter: the market is small, nobody cares that we lead, forget leadership and concentrate on selling the category's benefits. Their answer is never to forget leadership no matter how small the market, because a leadership position is hard to lose once held and because new prospects in a young category have no experience of it and gravitate to the leading brand — and one should never assume people know which brand leads. Their case is Datastream, which held 32 per cent of a very, very small maintenance-software market, promoted itself as the leader in all its literature, and still dominated once the market grew. On the sophisticated customers: they say that as a category matures the more adventurous buyers go out of their way not to buy the leader, and the instruction is blunt — write them off, you cannot appeal to everybody.
item.support: Printed pp. 31-33. The durability claim rests on "a widely publicized study of twenty-five leading brands . . . in the year 1923" with no author, title or method given — a third-party figure reported second-hand, not a measurement made by this book.
confounders: the category-education strategy of selling the category first in a new market, which is what the board proposes and what Chapter 8 recommends for a leader — the two chapters point differently here and the book does not reconcile them
assuming the small market makes the credential dishonest; the authors treat a true claim about a tiny market as fully usable, and say elsewhere they invented categories to create such claims
reading 'write them off' as segmentation advice; it is a refusal to chase a segment, which is the opposite

source_terms: a British team was able to reduce the incidence of accidents on a traffic circle in Florida by 95 per cent by placing the painted lines differently
In one Dutch town traffic experts improved traffic safety by removing road markings altogether.
item.claim: Behaviour in a physical environment responds to informational cues, and altering the cues can produce large effects without altering the structure. The source reports that a British team cut accidents on a Florida traffic circle by 95 per cent by placing the painted lines differently, and that traffic experts in a Dutch town improved safety by removing road markings altogether. It also notes that the original Clearwater design was not helped by a large decorative fountain in the middle, and that a later redesign reduced the accident rate significantly.

mechanism.text: Drivers act on how the environment reads to them, so the markings that convey the situation can matter more than the geometry they are painted on.

scope.conditions: environments where people respond to cues

caveats.text: The 95-per-cent figure is reported with no date, no baseline accident count, no comparison period and no citation. It is the largest single effect claimed anywhere in this section.

The two cases point in opposite directions — place the lines better, and remove them entirely — which fits the source's own thesis that opposites can both work, but means neither case supports a rule about markings.
The fountain claim and the redesign outcome are carried by the photograph's caption, not by the body text.

positive.description: the Clearwater traffic circle, photographed with its central decorative fountain

intra_source_relations.note: the worked instances of a psycho-logical problem

provenance.locator: Introduction, 'Context Is Everything', with the photograph and its caption

source_terms: it is not the consumer who has 'down-traded' but the supplier who has 'up-traded' his offer
item.claim: Bijapurkar identifies a specific misdiagnosis and corrects it. When richer consumers began buying popular-segment rather than premium products, marketers called this "down-trading" and "many have suggested that this is the nature of the Indian consumer — mean and stingy." Her correction: "In fact, it is not the consumer who has 'down-traded' but the supplier who has 'up-traded' his offer and the popular and discount segments, in many cases, now offer a real value advantage in terms of equivalent if not better benefits at a lower price." She supplies the supply-side cause: unequal tax and duty incentives were withdrawn, forcing small manufacturers into open competition, which produced "rogue" marketers who refused to respect the unwritten price-performance rules, so consumers faced an explosion of new price-performance combinations. She gives the automotive instances — a 125cc motorcycle at a 100cc popular price, premium styling at discount prices, a B- segment car with premium features — and concludes that "the paradigm of premium-popular-discount = rich-middle income-poor is now quite irrelevant."

mechanism.text: Observed behaviour changed because the choice set changed, not because preferences did. When the price-performance frontier moves, a buyer whose preferences are unchanged will appear at a different point on the old segmentation — and an analyst who holds the segmentation fixed will attribute the movement to the buyer's character.

scope.conditions: Indian consumer markets after the withdrawal of differential tax and duty structures, principally FMCG, automotive, PCs and industrial water treatment, over roughly 1991-2009.

caveats.text: THE GENERAL SHAPE IS THE VALUABLE PART AND IT IS NOT INDIAN. Attributing a shift in observed behaviour to consumer character when the choice set moved is a reasoning error available anywhere. The specific instances are dated
the cases are named products and are checkable in principle, but no market-share, price or volume data is given for any of them

the author also offers a second, different explanation elsewhere for the same FMCG stagnation — a 'change confluence' in which consumer credit and durables purchases committed future income, forcing careful FMCG spending. The two explanations are compatible but are not reconciled, and the book presents each as sufficient in its own place

INSPECTED: Figure 4.2, the premium-popular-discount construct, was opened. It is a schematic price-against-performance diagram showing the traditional line and three 'new offering' positions below it; it carries no data and is an illustration of the argument, not evidence for it

source_terms: an important difference between being far away from something and showing distance
a set of visual clues that show the viewer the distance between us and the subject
item.claim: The source separates two things routinely conflated. A telephoto lens deals with a far subject by bringing it closer in the frame and letting it be seen in more detail — a functional solution to being far away. What that can lose is any sense of distance, which the source says depends not on the lens but on a set of visual clues: ground visible continuously from the foreground to the subject, a slightly raised viewpoint that lets that ground be seen, aerial perspective, and here a sky of towering clouds that shows distance by standing over the mountains. It then qualifies itself — some telephoto shots do carry strong distance, when the viewpoint is high enough to see mountains arranged one behind another with haze at work — and concludes "it doesn't depend so much on the lens."

mechanism.text: Distance is inferred from a chain of intervening evidence. If the frame shows the whole ground between camera and subject, and shows atmosphere accumulating across it, the viewer can measure the gap; if the frame shows only the subject enlarged, there is nothing to measure against.

scope.conditions: The source's own frame is a wide-angle one (21mm equivalent on large format) from a slightly raised viewpoint with a lot of sky. Its qualification covers the telephoto case, so the claim is about cues and not about focal length either way.

caveats.text: The cue list is given as an account of one photograph rather than as an enumeration. It is not claimed to be complete and no cue is said to be necessary.

source_stated_problems: what may be missing from the equation is a sense of distance
source_stated_remedies: the viewpoint is slightly raised so that we can see from the foreground all the way to the mountains
taking in a lot of sky

positive.description: the Chisos Mountains across continuously visible ground, with tall cloud standing over them

counter.description: the telephoto solution that fills the frame with a far subject and loses the gap

item.source_locator: Ch. 4, section 'The Cultural Construction of Meaning', printed pp. 193-194
item.question: A distributor must design one key art for a film releasing simultaneously in six Indian language markets and in three diaspora territories. What does this source's account of text actually argue, and where does the argument stop being about India in 2002?
item.answer: The argument is not that posters look better without text; it is that TEXT PICKS A LANGUAGE AND PICKING A LANGUAGE CUTS THE AUDIENCE. With the scale of national and international distribution the Indian industry enjoys, 'text is seen as a cultural barrier', which is why Indian posters 'rarely use text' while contemporary Western posters carry substantial copy including review quotations acting as 'the media seal of approval'. So the reasoning transfers exactly to the case described: one artwork across nine markets is precisely the condition the convention was a response to, and every word added narrows it. What the source also supplies is what replaced the text — from the 1980s only the title and the names of the producer, director and music director, printed solely in English, because to the public those three names themselves signal the style, content and quality of the film. That second half is where the transfer stops. It depends on a star-and-credit system in which those three names carry meaning to that public, which is a fact about Indian audiences in a particular period and not a general property of names. In a diaspora territory whose audience does not hold that system, removing the text removes the signal and does not replace it, and the source says nothing about what would. Nothing here is measured either: no comparison of a text-carrying and a text-free poster is reported anywhere in the book.
item.support: 'text is seen as a cultural barrier'
item.confounders: Treating this as a minimalist design principle inverts it. The convention is a distribution constraint, and in a single-language market the constraint is absent.

item.source_locator: Ch. 4, section 'The Cultural Construction of Meaning', printed pp. 193-194
item.question: What contrast does the source draw between Indian and contemporary Western posters, and what reason does it give for the Indian side of it?
item.answer: Western posters present a dramatic enigma — provocative images and text giving incomplete or paradoxical information — which the public must see the film to resolve, and they are supported substantially by text, including review quotations that function as 'the media seal of approval' plus studio, producer and director credits signalling the film's status. Indian posters 'rarely use text'. The reason given is distribution: with the scale of national and international distribution the Indian industry enjoys, 'text is seen as a cultural barrier' — text picks a language, and picking a language cuts the audience. From the 1980s it has been more common for only the title and the names of the producer, director and music director to appear, printed solely in English, because to the public those three figures are themselves a marker of the style, content and quality of the film.
item.support: 'text is seen as a cultural barrier'
item.confounders: The absence of text is not an aesthetic preference in this account; it is a response to a multilingual distribution constraint, and the three names that DO appear are doing the work the review quotations do elsewhere.

source_terms: a color theme covers a number of images
photographers have to work with what is in front of them
the color palettes associated with places and with styles
item.claim: The source moves the unit of observation from the frame to the body of work. A colour theme, it says, covers a number of images and works well for a picture story because it holds them together and gives them unity — so it is a property of a set, not of a picture. It also removes the requirement of intent: the theme need not be planned, since it can simply be selected from what has already been shot. It then borrows palette from painting and marks the difference the borrowing conceals: for a painter the palette is an entirely personal decision, while a photographer has to work with what is in front of them, with processing able only to bend the situation. Its worked example treats a palette as a property of a place — New Mexico's earthen yellows, ochres and tans set against blue-greens — and it tests the claim on a street photograph, reporting the result as an opinion.

mechanism.text: Colours from one zone of the hue circle read as belonging together, so a run of images drawn from the same zone reads as a single body rather than as separate pictures.

scope.conditions: The theme example is a two-week assignment in which the source realised after the fact that the community lived within a certain range of colours. The claim is about a coherent assignment or story, not about arbitrary collections.

caveats.text: The palette test is reported as a self-assessment and hedged as one — "the colors, I think, hold up pretty well, too." No independent check is offered.

Attributing a palette to a place is a cultural and geographical generalisation, and the source's own supporting objects include deliberately self-conscious ones — art deco tiles that it says knowingly celebrate the palette in question.

you could simply select it from what you already shot

item.rationale: The Law of Color's operative property is not "is this colour good" but "is this colour held, and is it the one the competitor does not have". Both halves are relational and temporal. A single execution cannot answer either: a brand's colour is differentiating only relative to a named competitor's, and it is an asset only if it has been held long enough to be recognised, which is the whole of the source's Tiffany argument. So the honest observable is the colour distribution across a brand's output over a period, checked against the leading competitor's. Again a single asset cannot carry the property — every individual piece can be on-palette while the palette itself has been changing, or while it collides with the category leader's.

applicability.when: reviewing colour use across a brand's accumulated output over a period, with the competitor's palette available
applicability.limits: The source's rule is for a brand's whole visual identity, decided once and held for decades by a company, not for the palette of a production run. Its physiological justification — wavelengths focusing in front of or behind the retina, producing the emotional readings of red and blue — is offered without a source and does not support the cultural meanings the chapter derives from it. The colour associations listed are Western conventions. Nothing here should be applied to a brand whose market this project has not looked at.

item.source_locator: Ch. 3 'The Art of Advertising', printed pp. 101-182; thesis stated at p. 101
item.question: What is chapter 3's organising claim about how film-advertising style changed, and why does the Art Deco phase matter to that claim?
item.answer: That Indian film advertising did not evolve toward a single style but moved through distinct phases, each borrowing 'the aesthetic vocabulary of the period'. The sequence given: text-only newspaper notices and handbills from 1896; the Ravi Varma aesthetic, realist oil technique on Hindu mythological subject matter, carried into posters via the Varma press's oleographs; the Bombay School of Art style, a delicate realism tied to the Ajanta revival, used when a studio wanted to signal a film was special; Art Deco from the 1930s as a universal symbol of modernity; nationalist imagery around Independence, often using the map of India; overpainted montage in the 1970s-80s; computer-aided design from the 1990s. Art Deco matters because of how it ended: it 'did not survive beyond the end of the 1940s' in India because it came to be seen as Western cultural imperialism. That is a style displaced by a political meaning attaching to it rather than by a better style, which is the strongest evidence for the chapter's claim that these are period vocabularies rather than steps toward a solution.
item.support: each phase borrows 'the aesthetic vocabulary of the period'; Art Deco 'did not survive beyond the end of the 1940s'
item.confounders: Read as a progression toward better design, the sequence supports a 'this is how you make a film poster' conclusion. Read as the source states it, it supports the opposite: no phase here is the answer.

source_terms: each distinct phase in development marked a distinct aesthetic change in advertising
item.claim: Patel's organising claim for chapter 3 is that Indian film advertising did not evolve toward a single style but moved through distinct phases, each borrowing "the aesthetic vocabulary of the period." She sets out the sequence: text-only newspaper notices and handbills (1896 onward); the Ravi Varma aesthetic, realist oil technique applied to Hindu mythological subject matter, carried into posters via the Varma press's oleographs; the Bombay School of Art style, a delicate realism tied to Ajanta revival and used when a studio wanted to signal that a film was special; Art Deco from the 1930s as a universal symbol of modernity, which "did not survive beyond the end of the 1940s" in India because it was seen as Western cultural imperialism; nationalist imagery around Independence, often using the map of India; overpainted montage in the 1970s-80s; and computer-aided design from the 1990s.

mechanism.text: Patel's stated mechanism is that a style already carries associations before a poster uses it, so choosing a style is a way of saying something the image itself does not have to depict. She states it explicitly for the art-school style: it was "referred to whenever there was a need to communicate more than the basic information about a film," and in these instances "the mode of representation was often used to reflect or reinforce underlying messages about current cultural and political issues."

scope.conditions: Indian film advertising 1896-2002. Every phase is dated by the source. The claim is a periodisation, not a description of a standing style.

caveats.text: THIS IS THE OBJECT THAT PROTECTS THE REST FROM BEING FLATTENED. The source's own thesis is that the style changed repeatedly and that each change tracked a change in its environment. Any use of this book that produces a single timeless 'Indian poster style' contradicts the source's central argument
the mechanism — style carries prior association — is stated and illustrated but not tested; the source shows that designers used styles this way, not that audiences read them so
attributions are uneven: many booklets and posters of the period 'were unsigned', and Patel says so. Some phase-to-artist assignments therefore rest on stylistic attribution
